title: 53 comments on “How to Master Screenplay Structure: The #1 Technique Nobody Talks About”
use_cases: Use when you need to divide a screenplay into sequences that each reinforce a central theme.
Implement when positioning a midpoint scene to reset narrative momentum.
Configure when mapping scenes to sequence beats such as Call to Action, Act Break, and Climax.
Apply when preparing a structural outline during the drafting phase to ensure thematic coherence.
Use when revising a script to replace or relocate scenes that don’t serve the sequence’s story.
content:
1. Great Job with this article! One question...What do you do with scenes that can't carry an entire sequence, but are "story worthy" and belong in the script? Do you just insert them where you think they belong in one of the sequences? Thanks for your help.
Reply
2. Great Job! But...I have one question. In a sequence, must Every scene add to the theme of that particular sequence OR can one scene be placed in logical order of the total theme but not contribute much to that specific sequence story? Any help will be appreciated...thanks!
Reply Ideally every scene in the script - so in a sequence and the overall story - should relate back to the theme. A good exercise is to make a note of the theme as you watch a movie you've already seen and know what the theme is. If you stop it at random, is that scene serving the theme?
Reply

Is each of the sequence beats a scene? just a bit confused how the scenes play within the sequence...

30. Thanks for the feedback, Gabe - really appreciate it! Yes, you're right that the scenes within a sequence act as the Call to Action, Act Break, Midpoint etc. but there are usually more than seven scenes in a sequence. The very best way to get a handle on it is to write outlines of movies as you watch them, and then break down the outline into sequences and then see where the individual "plot point" scenes occur within the sequence.
